text: The oracle and diffusion operators from the previous lesson aren't abstract math you take on faith — they're built from ordinary gates: Hadamards and a multi-controlled phase flip. This lesson lays out the actual circuit, gate by gate.

At the top level, Grover's algorithm on n qubits is four steps. Start with n qubits all at zero. Apply a Hadamard to every qubit, producing the uniform superposition where every basis state has equal amplitude. Repeat t times: apply the oracle, then apply diffusion — that's where everything interesting happens. Then measure all n qubits, and with the right choice of t, you read out the marked state with high probability.

The oracle is built as X gates to align the target pattern, a multi-controlled-Z gate that flips the sign exactly when all qubits read 1, then X gates to undo the alignment. The diffusion operator needs to reflect about the uniform superposition, which isn't a convenient primitive — so instead you build the easy reflection about all-zeros, and sandwich it between two layers of Hadamards. Because Hadamard maps all-zeros exactly to the uniform superposition, that sandwich turns the easy reflection into exactly the one the algorithm needs, using only Hadamards, X gates, and multi-controlled-Z.

Each full iteration costs exactly one oracle call, since diffusion never touches the oracle, only the fixed all-zeros phase flip. Running t star equals floor of pi over 4 times root N iterations therefore costs exactly that many oracle calls total. Since t star scales as root N, this is the formal statement of Grover's quadratic speedup: O of root N oracle queries, versus O of N classically.
Next lesson puts real numbers behind t star — and shows why running more than t star iterations isn't a safety margin, it actively makes things worse.
